stories.headline: Oil plunges about 8% as the midterm rout raises hopes of an Iran exit, with Brent near $95
stories.dek: Democrats' sweep, a Vance post tying the losses to the war, and Trump playing down strikes cut the risk premium. One report put Brent at $94.62, its lowest close since Aug. 31.
tldr: Wednesday: oil fell roughly **8%**. One end-of-day report had Brent settling down $8.98 (8.7%) at **$94.62** and WTI down $7.97 (8.3%) at **$88.12**, both the lowest since Aug. 31.
Drivers: the Democratic sweep, a post from Vice President Vance tying the GOP defeat to the Iran war, and Trump saying he has no immediate plans to strike Iran.
Caveat: an Iranian official said the sides remain far apart, and a deal seen as a Trump defeat could provoke escalation. Oil has sold off on 'false dawns' before.
whatHappened: **Wednesday:** oil collapsed after the midterms. Democrats won both chambers, and traders read that as constraining the war and nudging Trump toward a deal. Vice President Vance publicly tied the Republican losses to the Iran conflict, which reports described as a key catalyst, and Trump said he had no immediate plans to strike Iran, so the sense of near-term escalation risk drained out of the market. An end-of-day report put Brent at $94.62 (down 8.7%) and WTI at $88.12 (down 8.3%), their lowest closes since Aug. 31; intraday moves varied widely, from about 2.5% early to 10% at the worst. Analysts warned the relief may not last: one Iranian official said the sides remain far from an agreement, and a deal framed as a defeat for Trump could provoke escalation.

**Monday:** oil dropped about 7% as Washington and Tehran both signaled room for diplomacy. Iranian President Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government 'certain authorities' over peace talks with the US, without spelling out their scope. A Qatari mediator traveled to Tehran to work on a draft agreement, and Iran's foreign minister said consultations were intensive. Trump told Axios he is in 'no rush' to decide on resuming strikes. Reports conflict on what comes after Tuesday's midterms: the Wall Street Journal has said he leans toward a large strike, while Middle East Eye quotes him saying he won't attack after the election. CNBC reported Brent settled down 7.6% at $104.77; Reuters had Brent near $104.96 and WTI near $96.62 at midday. Analysts quoted by CNBC said much of the recent rally was risk premium for escalation, and Raymond James' Pavel Molchanov said skepticism is warranted after many 'false dawns'.

**Weekend:** Iran's Revolutionary Guard said a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels hit a naval mine in Hormuz on Friday and caught fire. Washington disputed some mine claims earlier in the week, and Gulf allies were reportedly told to prepare for a possible round of strikes.
background:
- **Feb. 28:** US and Israeli strikes on Iran start the war, and Iran shuts the Strait of Hormuz to foreign shipping.
- **April:** A Pakistan-brokered ceasefire briefly reopens traffic. Talks in Islamabad fail, and the US blockades Iranian ports from mid-April to late May.
- **June:** A US–Iran memorandum is signed to formally end the conflict.
- **July 8:** The ceasefire collapses when Iran starts attacking commercial ships.
- **Since then:** Mediation (Qatar the main channel, Pakistan also active) has been on and off, with no breakthrough yet.

Why it's so big: before the war, roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil and a fifth of its LNG went through Hormuz. It's the ultimate [[chokepoint]]. When flows run at 60%, the barrels physically can't reach buyers, and prices carry a hefty war [[risk premium]] on top of the actual shortage.

This is a textbook [[supply shock]]. Prices rise because supply is squeezed, not because demand is booming, and that's why it's so awkward for central banks: it pushes inflation up *and* growth down at the same time.

grandLine.title: The Red Line crossing
grandLine.body: There are only two ways to get a ship across the Red Line: through Mary Geoise with the World Government's permission, or down through Fish-Man Island. Control those passages and you control trade between the seas. Hormuz is the oil world's Red Line crossing. How much oil exists on the far side barely matters. What matters is how much can get through, and right now that's about 60%.

whyItMatters: The [[pass-through]] to inflation is fast and visible: gasoline rose 9.1% in September and accounted for more than half of the CPI increase. That's what turned the Fed from cutting in 2025 to hiking in September.

Across assets: energy producers win; airlines, shippers and consumer names lose. Inflation [[breakevens]] rise, and long-term Treasury yields get an upward nudge. The big macro fear is [[stagflation]]: a central bank hiking into an energy shock that is already slowing the consumer.
Event risk now clusters around the midterms. If the reports of post-election strikes are right, the first week of November could bring another leg up in oil.

views.thesis: The market is genuinely short of oil, and the premium is justified.
views.argument: Flows are still well below prewar levels, inventories are being drawn down, and every diplomatic breakthrough has unraveled. Escalation (post-midterm strikes, attacks on Saudi infrastructure) remains plausible.
views.who: UBS, which sees ~$110 Brent at year-end.

views.thesis: A deal or demand destruction could deflate the premium quickly.
views.argument: Prices whip around with every diplomatic headline (Tuesday's drop shows how fast hope gets priced). Above $100, consumers cut back and the economy slows. The US administration has repeatedly called the war 'essentially over'. If shipping normalizes, much of the risk premium can come out fast.

views.thesis: The bigger risk is central banks overtightening into a supply shock.
views.argument: Oil at $115 is painful, but the danger for markets is the Fed (and ECB, and BoJ, which all hiked in September) tightening into an energy shock. That's how supply shocks turn into recessions, as in the 1970s and 2008.

interview.question: How does a war in the Middle East end up in US interest rates?
interview.answer: Through oil, then inflation, then the Fed. Hormuz is a [[chokepoint]] for about a quarter of seaborne oil. With flows at about 60%, Brent was above $100 for weeks (about $115 on Friday) and has now fallen to the mid-$90s on hopes of a deal, and gasoline drove more than half of September's 3.7% CPI. Normally the Fed would look through a [[supply shock]], but after most of a year of high energy prices it's worried about second-round effects, so it hiked in September and markets price another in December. That lifts the 2-year directly and adds inflation risk premium to the 10-year. What would reverse it is a credible deal that reopens the strait.

followUp.question: Why doesn't the Fed just 'look through' an oil shock?
followUp.answer: It can if the shock is short and expectations stay anchored. This one has lasted most of the year, core inflation is creeping up, and the risk is that higher prices get built into wages and expectations. At that point waiting is more expensive than acting. The Fed's credibility is the asset it's protecting.

trade.expression: Buy 5Y TIPS / sell 5Y nominal Treasuries (long the 5Y breakeven)
trade.rationale: [[breakevens|Breakevens]] measure the inflation rate markets expect. If energy stays tight and pass-through keeps showing up in CPI, inflation expectations rise and TIPS outperform nominal Treasuries. Owning the spread isolates the inflation view without taking a big bet on the level of rates.
risks: A real ceasefire reopens Hormuz and oil collapses, taking breakevens with it.
Demand destruction or recession knocks inflation expectations down.
Aggressive Fed hikes restore credibility and compress breakevens even while oil stays high.

keyTerms.definition: A narrow passage that a big share of global trade must go through, such as Hormuz, Suez or Malacca. Disruption there hits supply far beyond the region.
The extra price (or yield) markets charge for uncertainty, on top of fundamentals. In oil, it's the 'war premium' that can vanish on a peace deal.
A sudden drop in the supply of something important (here, oil) that raises prices and slows growth at the same time. It's hard for central banks, because the cure for inflation worsens the slowdown.
How much and how fast a cost change (oil, tariffs, the dollar) shows up in consumer prices.
keyTerms.example: Gasoline up 9.1% in September drove over half of the CPI gain.

keyTerms.definition: The inflation rate at which TIPS and regular Treasuries return the same: the nominal yield minus the TIPS (real) yield. It's the market's inflation expectation.
High inflation plus weak growth. It's the 1970s nightmare, and the toughest backdrop for both stocks and bonds.

watchNext.what: Does the relief hold? Watch Iran's response and Trump's next comments on strikes versus a deal.
Hormuz transits (~60% of normal) are the physical test; the price fell faster than the supply picture changed.

stories.headline: Dow jumps 3% for its best day since April 2025 as oil plunges after the Democratic sweep
stories.dek: Stocks rallied hard Wednesday: the S&P 500 had its best day in three months and the Nasdaq rose 1.4%. Thursday brings the Bank of England; Friday, payrolls.
tldr: **Wednesday close:** the Dow rose 3.03% (+1,569) to **53,356.12**, the S&P 500 1.58% to **7,688.62**, and the Nasdaq 1.44% to **25,736.51**; the Dow's best day since April 9, 2025.
**Why:** Democrats won Congress and oil plunged on Iran-exit hopes, easing both political and inflation worries.
**Still ahead:** Thu Bank of England; Fri payrolls (consensus ~+55k, 4.2% unemployment). I couldn't confirm the outcome of Wednesday's Treasury refunding.
whatHappened: Stocks surged the day after the midterms. The Dow gained 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, to 53,356.12, its best day since April 9, 2025; the S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,688.62, its best day in three months; and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44% to 25,736.51, with the Nasdaq-100 up 0.91% as chips lagged. Oil's roughly 8% drop (see the oil story) and the sweep's gridlock implications drove the move. Tuesday's Investing.com/Yahoo figures were intraday; these are closing levels from several recaps.

I could not find the content of Wednesday's Treasury [[quarterly refunding]] announcement, only Treasury's August guidance that coupon sizes would stay unchanged for at least several quarters, so check the Treasury release. Next: the Bank of England Thursday and Friday's jobs report, the last before the Fed's Dec. 8–9 meeting.
background: Why the refunding matters: when deficits are large, Treasury decides how much to borrow in long bonds versus short bills. More long-dated supply means investors must absorb more duration, which pushes up term premium; leaning on bills does the opposite. It was a big driver of the 10-year's climb toward 5.35% earlier this month.
whyItMatters: Two questions for the week: does the AI selloff become a broader de-risking (watch Apple and AMD), and does Friday's payrolls print change December? A soft jobs number plus falling oil would chip at the ~80–86% December hike pricing; a firm one with oil above $100 keeps the hawks in charge.

views.thesis: The AI rout is a valuation reset in a strong economy.
views.argument: GDP grew 3.4%, breadth was positive on Thursday, and most stocks aren't AI spenders. Rotation into small caps and cyclicals can continue even if megacaps stay weak.

views.thesis: Event risk is stacked: election, war, jobs, refunding.
views.argument: A post-election Iran strike, hawkish refunding or a hot payrolls number could hit bonds and stocks together. With megacap sentiment broken, there's little cushion.

interview.question: What's the single most important event for markets this week?
interview.answer: Friday's payrolls. The election is largely priced and the refunding is usually telegraphed, but jobs decide December: the market prices roughly an 80–86% chance of a hike, and a weak print with oil easing would chip at that, while a firm one keeps the front end pinned. The wildcard is oil, if the US resumes strikes on Iran right after the vote.

followUp.question: What would you watch in the refunding?
followUp.answer: Whether Treasury keeps saying coupon sizes stay steady for several quarters. Any hint of larger long-bond auctions would add supply and push term premium up.

keyTerms.definition: Treasury's announcement, each February, May, August and November, of how much it will borrow and in which maturities over the coming quarter.
keyTerms.example: The Nov. 4 refunding will show whether coupon auction sizes stay steady.

stories.headline: Democrats win control of the House and Senate; stock futures dip, then recover
stories.dek: Maine's Susan Collins lost and the Senate flipped. Nasdaq futures fell as much as 2.4% overnight on AI-regulation worries before recovering by morning.
tldr: **Democrats won both chambers**, per CNN, CBS, CNBC and Yahoo projections; Alaska and Mississippi were still uncalled and seat counts may change.
Cash markets: the Dow rose 3.03% and the S&P 500 1.58% on Wednesday after overnight futures dipped (Nasdaq-100 futures fell as much as 2.4%) and then recovered.
Long-dated Treasury yields eased on gridlock expectations; chip stocks like Nvidia and Micron dipped over AI-oversight worries while AMD rose about 6% on earnings.
whatHappened: Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterms, according to projections from CBS (shortly after 11:30 p.m. ET), CNN, CNBC and Yahoo. Flipped Senate seats included Maine, where Susan Collins was defeated, with Texas and Kansas among the other flips reported. CNN said Alaska and Mississippi were too early to call and CNBC called Alaska neck and neck, so the final tallies may move. Democrats gain subpoena power for investigations. President Trump congratulated Democrats but said he does not see the result as a rejection of his leadership.

Markets: US stock futures fell sharply as the results came in, with Nasdaq-100 futures down as much as 2.4% and S&P 500 futures 1.4% at the worst, then recovered; by Wednesday morning reports had Dow futures up about 0.6% and S&P futures up about 0.2%. Investors worried that tougher congressional scrutiny could slow the AI build-out, and chip stocks including Nvidia and Micron fell more than 1% in early trading. Long-dated Treasury yields moved lower as investors weighed the effect of gridlock on government spending. I couldn't confirm any dollar move.
background: Midterms usually go against the president's party, and prediction markets had a Democratic sweep at roughly 70% going in, so the headline was largely [[priced in]]. What was less priced was the AI-regulation angle, which explains why tech futures took the brunt overnight.
A Democratic Congress means [[gridlock]] on big spending or tax bills, but the White House still controls tariffs, foreign policy and the Iran war.
whyItMatters: For rates, a divided government limits new deficit-financed packages, which at the margin is a small positive for the long end and term premium. For equities, the risk is sector-specific: AI and data-center names face more oversight and subpoenas, while defense and energy depend on the White House's choices. Oil and trade risks don't change with the House gavel.

views.thesis: A split government caps fiscal surprises and tends to calm markets.
views.argument: With Democrats controlling Congress, major tax and spending bills stall. That means less extra Treasury supply, a modest positive for bonds in a year when deficits pushed the 10-year toward 5%, and the quick futures recovery fits that view.

views.thesis: The overnight tech selloff is the real signal.
views.argument: Subpoena power and committee hearings raise the political cost of data-center build-outs and AI deals. Investors worried that greater scrutiny could slow the industry's expansion, hitting the suppliers and spenders already stressed in October.

views.thesis: Oil and the Fed matter far more than Congress.
views.argument: The war with Iran and an inflation-sensitive Fed dominate the macro picture; election outcomes were largely priced, and within days the focus returns to payrolls and energy.

interview.question: Democrats just won both chambers. How do you trade it?
interview.answer: Lightly. It was roughly 70% [[priced in]], and the futures round trip shows the headline faded fast. My view is it's a small positive for the long end because [[gridlock]] limits new deficit spending, and a sector story for AI names facing oversight. The real swing factors are still oil and Friday's payrolls. I'd change my mind if the new Congress moves on tariffs or AI rules faster than expected.

followUp.question: Why did futures fall overnight and then recover?
followUp.answer: Early results suggested a bigger Democratic win than some expected, and AI names took the hit. Then investors reassessed: gridlock limits legislation, and strong earnings like AMD's steadied sentiment.

keyTerms.definition: When the White House and Congress (or the two chambers) are controlled by different parties, so little major legislation passes.
Already reflected in market prices, so it won't move markets when it happens.
keyTerms.example: A Democratic sweep was about 70% priced before election night.

watchNext.what: Treasury's quarterly refunding and ISM services; the Alaska and Mississippi Senate calls.
October payrolls, the next macro swing.

grandLine.title: A Reverie that rewrites the rules
grandLine.body: Every four years the world's kings gather at Reverie and can abolish a whole system, as they did with the Seven Warlords. A midterm that flips Congress is a smaller version: it can't rewrite the whole order, but it can change who gets investigated, funded and licensed. Markets didn't panic about the World Government; they repriced the part of the sea where the new rules might bite, which is AI.

trade.rationale: Gridlock limits new deficit-financed supply, so long-end term premium can ease (long yields fell overnight) while the Fed stays hawkish at the front end. That flattens the 2s10s curve. This is interview framing, not advice.
risks: An oil spike lifts inflation expectations and long yields anyway.
A refunding that adds coupon supply swamps the gridlock story.
If the Fed turns dovish, the front end rallies and the curve steepens.

stories.headline: Apple beats on revenue and EPS in Ternus's first report, but shares fall on a weak margin outlook
stories.dek: Revenue rose 12% to $114.48B and iPhone set a September-quarter record, yet the stock was down about 2% midday Tuesday as guidance disappointed.
tldr: Revenue **$114.48B (+12%)** vs. about $113.4B expected; EPS **$2.10** vs. about $1.99; iPhone **$57.58B (+17%)**.
Shares fell in late trading as the margin forecast for the holiday quarter disappointed, per CNBC and SiliconANGLE.
It's the first earnings call under CEO John Ternus, and the first big test of whether the market still pays for AI-era hardware after October's tech rout.
whatHappened: Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results Monday after the close. Revenue rose 12% to $114.48 billion, above the roughly $113.4 billion analysts expected, and adjusted EPS was $2.10 versus a consensus near $1.99. iPhone revenue was $57.58 billion, up 17% and ahead of the $56.5 billion estimate, a September-quarter record. Coverage said the quarter contained only a handful of days of new iPhone sales, so the holiday quarter carries the weight. The stock fell in late trading on a [[gross margin]] forecast that came in light, with [[guidance]] for the December quarter the main swing factor. I couldn't confirm the size of the after-hours move or the exact guidance figures; check Apple's release.
background: Apple has leaned on iPhone upgrade cycles and high-margin Services to defend its margins against rising memory-chip and tariff costs. A new CEO makes guidance more scrutinized, because the market is judging whether the post-transition playbook holds.
whyItMatters: Apple is the largest weight in the major equity indexes, so a guidance-driven slide matters for the Nasdaq the morning after. It also reinforces the October theme: investors are rewarding cash generation and punishing spending or margin pressure, whatever the headline beat.

grandLine.title: Big News Morgans and the headline
grandLine.body: The World Economy News Paper's boss famously spins a headline to sell papers. A 'beat' is the headline; guidance is the fine print. Markets trade the fine print, because a beat tells you what already happened, and guidance tells you what they'll be paying for next.

views.camp: Beat now, margin worry is fixable
views.thesis: The quarter was strong and the margin dip is cost timing.
views.argument: Revenue and iPhone both beat, and memory costs could ease. A small post-earnings dip after a record iPhone quarter is a chance to buy.

views.thesis: The weak margin outlook is the signal, not the beat.
views.argument: With tariffs and memory costs rising, a light gross-margin forecast suggests earnings power is peaking, which matters most for a stock priced for steadiness.

interview.question: Apple beat on revenue and EPS but the stock fell after hours. Why?
interview.answer: Because the market trades the forward numbers, not the print. A beat was expected, and the [[gross margin]] outlook came in light, so earnings estimates for the next quarter go down. My view is the reaction is about guidance, not the quarter. What would change my mind is if management shows the margin pressure is a one-off, like memory costs reversing.

followUp.question: What would you look at to tell if it's a buying opportunity?
followUp.answer: Services growth and gross margin trend, because they drive earnings quality. And I'd compare the move to peers: if the whole megacap group is falling on AI-spending worries, it's sector, not Apple.

keyTerms.definition: Revenue minus cost of goods sold, as a percent of revenue. Rising component or tariff costs squeeze it.
keyTerms.example: Apple's outlook for gross margin is the swing factor this quarter.

keyTerms.definition: A company's own forecast for coming-quarter revenue, margins or EPS. Stocks often move more on guidance than on the quarter just reported.

watchNext.what: How Apple opens after the report, and whether the Nasdaq follows.
Payrolls, the next macro swing for megacap valuations.

stories.headline: Palantir revenue jumps 96% to $2.31B, its first quarter above $2 billion
stories.dek: U.S. commercial sales passed U.S. government sales for the first time, a key test of the AI-software story after October's tech rout.
tldr: Revenue **$2.313B**, up **96%** year over year and 20% from the prior quarter, above the company's own $2.16B guidance.
GAAP and adjusted EPS were both **$0.44**; adjusted free cash flow was **$1.216B**.
U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time. The stock was among the S&P 500's larger decliners Tuesday morning.
whatHappened: Palantir's Q3 press release (filed with the SEC) shows revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% from a year earlier and 20% from the second quarter, and the first quarter above $2 billion. GAAP and adjusted EPS were both $0.44, adjusted [[free cash flow]] was $1.216 billion, and cash plus Treasuries stood at $10.4 billion. U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time. The shares traded lower Tuesday despite the beat, a reminder of how much was priced in. I found no reliable coverage of any change to full-year guidance, so check the release before quoting it.
background: Palantir is the market's favorite proxy for 'AI that actually makes money', so it trades at a premium multiple. That means the reaction depends on whether growth beats what is already [[priced in]], not on whether it was good.
whyItMatters: After October's selloff in AI-spending names, a profitable, fast-growing software name is a counterpoint to the 'AI cash burn' story that hit Alphabet, Intel and Amazon. A strong print helps the argument that AI demand is real. A fade says expectations were too high.

grandLine.title: Nami reads the sky
grandLine.body: Nami doesn't wait for the storm to hit; she reads small signs in the air. A commercial business overtaking government sales is that kind of sign: it shows demand coming from customers who pay on their own, not just from a single large patron. Traders read the sign before the weather shows up in the earnings.

views.thesis: 96% growth with real cash flow earns a premium.
views.argument: Revenue is accelerating, margins are positive and U.S. commercial demand is now the larger engine, which makes growth less dependent on government budgets.

views.thesis: Even a big beat may not be enough at this valuation.
views.argument: A stock at a steep multiple needs growth to keep outrunning expectations. History shows premium software names can fall on beats if guidance or the pace of acceleration only matches the whisper number.

interview.question: Palantir grew revenue 96%. Why might the stock still fall?
interview.answer: Because the move depends on expectations, not the print. At a premium multiple the beat is [[priced in]], so the stock needs guidance or acceleration to surprise too. My view is that the quality is strong, with U.S. commercial now larger than government, but the risk is multiple compression if growth slows. I'd change my mind if guidance implies a deceleration or free cash flow falls.

followUp.question: What does U.S. commercial overtaking government tell you?
followUp.answer: That demand is broadening beyond a single, budget-driven customer, which lowers concentration risk and supports the idea that enterprises will pay for AI software.

keyTerms.definition: Cash from operations minus capital spending: what the business generates that could fund buybacks, dividends or acquisitions.
keyTerms.example: Palantir's adjusted free cash flow was $1.216B.

keyTerms.definition: A piece of news is priced in when the market already expects it, so the stock moves only on the surprise.
keyTerms.example: A 96% growth print can still disappoint if the market expected faster.

watchNext.what: How PLTR trades at the open and whether the AI-software group follows.

stories.headline: AMD beats on revenue and earnings, with data-center sales up 97%; shares jump after hours
stories.dek: The chipmaker's report on Election Day is another read on AI demand after Apple and Palantir, and shares rose roughly 7–8% in extended trading.
tldr: AMD beat Wall Street's revenue and EPS expectations for the third quarter, per reports.
**Data-center revenue rose 97%** year over year, the main driver.
Shares rose roughly **6%** in premarket Wednesday after a 7–8% after-hours gain. I couldn't confirm the exact revenue, EPS or guidance numbers.
whatHappened: AMD reported third-quarter results after the closing bell Tuesday, beating expectations on the top and bottom lines. Data-center revenue grew 97% from a year earlier, the standout line as investors look for proof that AI spending turns into sales. The stock rose roughly 7–8% in extended trading, which fits with chip stocks having rallied in the regular session. I couldn't verify the exact revenue and EPS figures or the fourth-quarter outlook, so check AMD's release before quoting them.
background: After October's AI selloff hit Alphabet, Intel and Amazon on spending worries, the market has been sorting AI names into those making money from the build-out and those paying for it. A chipmaker whose data-center sales nearly doubled sits on the 'selling the picks and shovels' side.
whyItMatters: A strong print supports the [[AI capex]] trade and helps the Nasdaq after a rough month. The catch is positioning: a stock that has rallied into earnings needs the outlook, not just the quarter, to beat.

grandLine.title: The Sabaody bubble coating
grandLine.body: At Sabaody, resin bubbles let ships dive deeper than they otherwise could, until the pressure gets too high and the coating pops. AI spending is the coating: it carries the whole sector deeper, and chipmakers sell the resin. Strong data-center growth shows the dive is still going well; the risk is what happens if the customers paying for it run short of cash.

views.thesis: Data-center revenue near doubling shows AI spending is still accelerating.
views.argument: Cloud and enterprise buyers are still ordering accelerators, so chip suppliers keep benefiting even as their customers face questions about returns.

views.thesis: A one-day gain after a beat tells you little about durability.
views.argument: After October's selloff, sentiment swings fast. If hyperscaler cash burn forces capex cuts, the suppliers feel it with a lag.

interview.question: AMD's data-center revenue is up 97% and the stock jumped. How do you think about it?
interview.answer: It's a supplier benefiting from customers' [[AI capex]]. The print is good, but the question is durability. My view is that demand holds through the next few quarters, and the risk is customers cutting spending if returns disappoint. I'd change my mind if guidance implies growth slowing or if hyperscalers trim capex.

followUp.question: Why did chip stocks rally while Apple fell?
followUp.answer: Apple's issue was margins and a cost squeeze on a mature product. Chips are riding the spending boom. It's the same theme viewed from the two ends: who gets paid versus who pays.

keyTerms.definition: Capital spending by cloud and tech companies on data centers, chips and power for AI. It is revenue for suppliers like AMD and a cash drain for the spenders.
keyTerms.example: October's selloff hit names seen as burning cash on AI capex.
